findings.what: The screen's key claim, "A run of 1 gives a rise of 2, which is m itself" (the brief's promised run-of-1 step), shows only mid-slide: its triangle and its working "m = (7 − 5) ÷ (3 − 2) = 2 ÷ 1 = 2" are at full strength from 2.2 s to 2.6 s, then fade and slide away, and the screen settles on the (0, 1) to (5, 11) triangle. Reorder the keys so the slide ends on (2, 5) to (3, 7) (big, bigger, then the run of 1), so the picture Dan is left with is the one the last sentence names.

The big triangle's points carry their coordinates, (2, 5) and (5, 11), and its rise arrow reaches the grid line at 11, so Dan can get 6 by working out 11 − 5 without using the climb for each 1 along that the puzzle names. Hide the top point's label ("?") until Check or Why? so the puzzle tests that idea.

It defines m as the climb for each 1 along and then does 6 ÷ 3 = 2, but the screen never joins the two (6 up over 3 along is 2 up for each 1 along); that joining sentence is only in the explain. Add "so it climbs 2 for each 1 along" so the screen gives the why as well as the sum.

findings.where: Step 9 text, step 10 Why?, explain paragraph 3
findings.what: "Nothing can be divided by 0" is stated without a reason. One first-principles clause would close it, for example "no number times a run of 0 gives a rise of 5" or "steps of 0 along never climb 5".

The triangle here is 3 squares by 3 squares, so counting squares gives 1 while the scales give 5 V per A. That is the best place to name the counting-squares slip (now only in the practice list and the ignores note), and no puzzle offers that slip (the tank's square count would be 0.5). One sentence on the screen would teach it where it can be seen.

findings.where: Steps 5-6 (falling line) and 11-12 (units, tank in litres per minute)
findings.what: The brief lists Δy ÷ Δx with units and a falling graph's minus sign as not to be taught again (Calculus fundamentals lesson 1, which also used a tank in litres per minute). The screens re-teach them in full and never say he has met them. A one-line "you met this as a falling rate in Calculus fundamentals" on steps 5 and 11 would make them recognition, not repetition.

"A price only goes up as you buy more" can be read as the price per metre rising, which clashes with the next sentence about a cheaper full drum. "The total cost only goes up as you buy more" keeps the break true and clear.

"When the course's winding readings ... plot roughly as a line" points at readings Dan has not met yet (lesson 5). Say it is coming later, for example "In lesson 5, a copper winding's resistance against temperature ...".

findings.where: Step 1 label A (1, 3); step 13 label A (−3, 4)
findings.what: Both point labels sit about a square and a half from their dots, above-left across the y-axis on step 1 and below on step 13, so they float rather than sit beside the point. They are legible and carry their coordinates, but a closer spot would read better.

Draggable A and B look the same as the fixed puzzle points, and only step 1's text says they can be dragged. A faint ring on draggable points would show the thing to move on every screen that allows it.

findings.where: Puzzle screens at 360 px (for example steps 2 and 13)
findings.what: The readout keeps a blank second line under "m = ?", and the empty feedback line leaves a band of about 70 px between Check/Why? and Back. Both are there on purpose so nothing jumps, but on a phone the puzzle looks unfinished before Check. A shorter reserved height on puzzles would tighten it.
